"Hopper" is a noun with several distinct meanings. They can be grouped into two broad families: things that hop, and things shaped like a funnel or chute.

A hopper is any creature or person that moves by hopping or jumping.

  • A grasshopper is sometimes called simply a "hopper," especially in casual or regional speech. Farmers might say "the hoppers are destroying the wheat" to mean a swarm of grasshoppers.
  • More generally, a child jumping around could be called a little hopper, though this use is informal and not very common.
Family 2 — A funnel-shaped container that feeds material downward

This is by far the most important and widely used meaning of the word.

A hopper is a large, open container — wide at the top, narrow at the bottom — designed to hold loose bulk material (like grain, coal, sand, cement, gravel, or seeds) and release it in a controlled flow through an opening or gate at the bottom. Think of it like an upside-down pyramid or a funnel with steep walls.

The key idea is: you load material in from the top, and it flows or drops out from the bottom when you're ready.

You find hoppers everywhere in industry and agriculture:

  • A grain hopper at a farm holds harvested wheat or corn and feeds it steadily into a processing machine below.
  • A cement hopper on a construction site holds dry cement and releases measured amounts into a mixer.
  • A coal hopper at a power plant holds coal and delivers it onto conveyor belts leading to the furnace.
  • A sand hopper at a foundry meters out sand for mold-making.

The design is intentional — the sloped, angled walls prevent material from getting stuck and ensure it slides down toward the outlet by gravity alone.
Specific things called a "hopper" in different contexts

Because the funnel-and-feed idea is so useful, the word gets applied in many specific settings:

1. Hopper car (railroads)
A railroad freight car with a built-in hopper bottom — the floor slopes inward toward openings underneath, so the car can be loaded from the top (with coal, grain, or gravel) and unloaded simply by opening the bottom hatches and letting gravity do the work. You'll hear this called a hopper car or just a hopper.

2. Paper hopper (printers and office machines)
The tray or slot on a printer, photocopier, document scanner, or card-sorting machine where you load the paper or cards before they are fed into the machine. The machine picks up sheets one by one from this tray. Office workers often say "the hopper is empty" when the printer runs out of paper. Some also call it an input hopper to distinguish it from the output tray.

3. Legislative hopper (politics/government)
In the United States Congress and many state legislatures, the hopper is the physical box or slot (often a wooden box fixed to the side of a desk or railing) where members of Congress formally deposit a bill to introduce it for consideration. When a politician "drops a bill in the hopper," it means they've officially submitted it. The phrase "in the hopper" has also entered everyday English as an idiom meaning something is in the pipeline — submitted, queued up, and waiting to be processed.

4. Drainage hopper / hopper head (plumbing and construction)
A funnel-shaped fitting, usually made of metal, attached to the top of a drainpipe or downspout on the outside of a building. It collects rainwater flowing off roofs or overflows from pipes and channels it into the vertical drain below. You'll see these on the exterior walls of older brick buildings.

5. Toilet hopper (British/Australian informal)
In older or informal British and Australian usage, a hopper can refer to a toilet — specifically, a type of toilet bowl shaped somewhat like a funnel (wide at the top, tapering down). This use is not very common today but you may encounter it in older literature or speech.

Because a hopper is a holding vessel where things wait before being processed, English picked up the phrase "in the hopper" to mean being worked on, in progress, or queued up for attention.

  • "We have three new projects in the hopper." → Three projects are lined up and being worked on.
  • "The proposal is still in the hopper." → The proposal has been submitted and is waiting to move forward.

This is a very common business and journalism expression.
The one thread connecting almost everything

Whether it's a giant coal container on a train, a paper tray on a printer, or a box in Congress — nearly every meaning of hopper shares this core logic:

A hopper receives things in bulk, holds them temporarily, and releases or delivers them in a controlled way.

Once you see that pattern, the word clicks into place across all its uses.
